description:
We’re tackling Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots: 

I’m a final-year AI & ML student at TU Dublin with experience in data pipelines and time-series analysis (Python, PostgreSQL). I’ll handle data cleaning and the harmonization itself.

Looking for: data scientists / analysts (statistics, time series, anomaly detection), someone strong in data visualization, and ideally a frontend or full-stack dev for the interactive map. No fire or remote sensing expertise needed, just message me!
summary: Satellites have mapped wildfires since 2000, but the record is split between two witnesses: MODIS (Terra, Aqua), nearing retirement, and its successor VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21). VIIRS sees smaller fires, so the raw counts of the two sensors can't be compared, and long-term trends break where one hands over to the other. We developed Flame Nebula, a web app that harmonizes both records into one consistent 25-year fire history and makes it usable in seconds. A user picks any area (a region by name, or a shape drawn on the map) and gets a burning activity calendar, area statistics, year-to-year comparison, recurring fire patterns and downloadable data. This answers the challenge directly: the sensor of origin no longer matters, and patterns, trends and anomalies become the focus. It matters because emergency responders, firefighters, land managers and scientists need to know when and where fire comes back, and a broken record hides exactly that.
details:
What it does: You open a full-screen satellite map and pick an area in one of four ways: draw a rectangle, circle or polygon, enter latitude/longitude with a radius, or search for a region by name. Then you choose a year, the sensors (MODIS, VIIRS or both), the fire type and day or night. The app shows:

- hotspots as heat-coloured bubbles that group when zoomed out and never overlap; you can click one to see its details;

- a burning activity calendar (month × day heatmap) with tooltips;

- stats: the number of hotspots and the total fire power (FRP) and most fire intense month;

- a Compare mode: two years side by side with a swipe divider, bar charts and % change;

- a Patterns layer: places where fire comes back in the same month in at least 12 of 14 years;

- a confidence score for each hotspot, plus a filter that hides likely non-fires (factories, gas flares, volcanoes).

You can download the selected hotspots as CSV or GeoJSON.

How it works: A Python pipeline fetch and cleans the FIRMS data. It removes static heat sources with a mask, assigns each hotspot to a country, and fits one calibration chain (Terra → Aqua → S-NPP → NOAA-20) for each country and month. That chain turns MODIS and VIIRS hotspots into one comparable unit. Each hotspot also gets a confidence score from up to 10 checks: product confidence, a VIIRS cross-check, land cover, MCD64A1 and EFFIS burned areas, smoke and CO, Landsat. The data goes into PostgreSQL, an Express API serves it, and a React app shows it.

Benefits and impact: Firefighters, emergency responders, land managers , risk agencies and scientists get 25 years of fire history for their own area in seconds. They can see which months burn most, which years were worse, and where fires come back every year. This helps them plan prevention and resources before the fire season starts.

Tools: Python 3.12 (pandas), PostgreSQL 17, Node 20 + Express, React 19 + TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind v4, shadcn/ui, Leaflet with Esri satellite tiles, Docker Compose, nginx, GitHub Actions, and Playwright for end-to-end tests. Data comes from NASA FIRMS, MCD64A1, EFFIS, Landsat, Planetary Computer and Worldview. No special hardware: just laptops and one cloud server.

What's creative: Instead of one simple fire count, we rate how sure we are that each hotspot is a real fire, using several independent sources. The Patterns layer turns 14 years of data into a map of where fire comes back. The swipe compare mode shows the difference between two years at a glance.

Factors we considered: MODIS and VIIRS detect fires differently: VIIRS sees more and smaller fires, and the MODIS fire-type field changed in 2018. False positives from factories and volcanoes and off-shore spills. Also covered days with missing satellite coverage. Speed: the map loads only the visible area, and the server caches responses. Accessible colour ramps. App is responsible on apps for the landfield workers. App allows to download formats (CSV, GeoJSON) that work in QGIS and ArcGIS.
